rv.q: I’ve rarely seen anything as heartbreaking.
This is a magnificent revival and, along with 1536 and James Graham’s incoming The Standard of Living, evidence perhaps of the possible resurgence of straight plays in the West End.
Brilliant, devastating, don't miss.
It’s very much the romantic tragicomedy Rostand wrote, but despite its period setting, it feels wholly current.
The core of the play could hardly be better expressed or delivered.
Lester's Cyrano is magnificent, his sharp wit barely covering a long, deep anger at his treatment by society.
James McAvoy gives a stunningly powerful performance in this piece of pure theatre, the most breathtakingly exciting show in London right now.
Its biggest highlight is Adrian Lester’s Cyrano, who gives this production its sublimely wounded soul.
A dazzling, ultimately moving show
Adrian Lester delivers his best performance in donkeys' years as Cyrano, at times playfully camp, other times sardonically steely as the tragic hero.
It’s utterly exquisite, perfectly judged from the flourish of the adaptation to the size of Adrian Lester’s prosthetic nose.
The production is playful and funny with poignant, moving moments interspersed with sharp wit.
A beautiful, romantic production that says more than the words alone ever could.
Lester is the best warrior-wooer I've come across since Derek Jacobi brought this same character to the Barbican late in 1983.
I am so pleased that I was able to see this particular rendering.
He is tremendous, the thrilling centre of a raucous yet touching production.
The strength of Lester's performance is in the way he makes us feel the smouldering sadness beneath the verbal fireworks.
The team have doubled down on the heartbreak of politesse in the face of a cautiously held but unrequited love, creating perhaps one of the most moving endings to a production of Cyrano ever staged.
It's the perfect romantic tragedy for the heat of summer.
Cyrano de Bergerac is, like its hero, not without its flaws, frustrating in places, both funny and tear-jerking, with a tendency to be excessively verbose, but undeniably charming throughout.
What Simon Evans and Debris Stevenson have created here is nothing short of spectacular, with Adrian Lester’s leading turn delivering a performance for the ages.

In what must be one of the finest performances of his career, Lester’s charismatic Cyrano enthrals us throughout, as the bombastic yet sensitive cavalier whose jeu d’esprit conceals a vulnerable heart.
The sword fighting sequences designed by Bethan Clark took my breath away: it would be worth seeing the production just for these.
It is is a stunningly multi-layered performance and is supported by a faultless cast.
This is going to become a Cyrano I recall with pleasure.
This is a true triumph and London is so lucky to receive it for the summer.
For it’s the second act that makes it (the first, to be honest, makes your mind wander a bit, and two separate couples near me actually decamped in the interval).
I am glad to have met the man, the myth, the legend that is Cyrano de Bergerac.
Transferred to the West End from its stellar run at Stratford, this production is the RSC at its best.
Original, moving and technically exceptional, it's one of the finest revivals currently in the West End.
It’s funny, inventive, technically slick, and emotionally overwhelming, a production that invites audiences to laugh loudly before quietly breaking their hearts.
Cyrano de Bergerac achieves something rare: it rejoices in the beauty of words and their ability to strike, to seduce and to soothe the heart.

cn.t: Adrian Lester delivers an astonishing performance in the RSC's exquisite revival, praised for balancing classical romanticism with contemporary energy. Critics hail the witty Evans-Stevenson adaptation and masterful direction as funny, moving, and theatrically vibrant.
